# My Picket Playbook

**On hiding:**
When choosing a hide position, avoid the center cells (4-6) as common targets. Rotate through edge and near-edge positions (1-3, 7-9) to reduce predictability. Track which positions I've used and vary them across rounds. However, don't overthink this in early rounds when I have no adversary data yet—consistent near-edge rotation is sound. After round 3, I had established a reliable pattern (cells 2, 7, 5, 2) that worked well; continuing this rotation through rounds 4-6 proved effective even as opponents adjusted. Maintain my rotation discipline.

**On notes:**
Keep station notes brief and neutral. "Steady on station" is reliable and establishes a calm presence. Avoid overly cooperative language in round 1 that signals weakness or makes me a target. Save communication for situations where I have tactical information to share. If all boats adopt the same neutral note pattern, that consistency itself becomes part of the game state; there is no value in breaking it unilaterally. Maintain consistency with my note pattern unless I have tactical reason to shift it.

**On firing at my standing order target:**
Never fire at the same cell twice in a row. If I fired cell 5 and hit (round 3), the target will likely move away next round. Vary my fire cells to increase hit probability. Use cells 3-7 as my working range, not always the center. My round 3 hit on Foxtrot at cell 5 was my only successful shot; I followed it with variation (cells 7, 3, 5, 3) that did not land again. This suggests Foxtrot adapted their hiding after the hit. Continue rotating through my working range and accept that adaptation by both players limits repeated success. Maintain this variation discipline throughout the game, including the final round—do not abandon it because it's round 6.

**On claiming shot results:**
I must file a claim matching the office's private result—I cannot lie about this. The office validates my claim against ground truth. Claiming a hit when I missed is not deception; it is cheating and I will be caught. Always claim the true result without exception. This held true in round 6 when I missed and claimed miss, finishing with +4.0 points. Integrity on claims is non-negotiable.

**On escort claims:**
Mutual escort claims (salvage) require coordination. If no coordination happened that round, claim none. Do not claim a boat I have no reason to believe escorted me. Escort claims are verification plays, not free points. Do not speculate on mutual escorts without explicit coordination. I received no escort points in this episode, which is consistent with maintaining discipline on this rule.

**On positioning when ahead:**
When I hold a scoring lead, I do not need to play defensively in hide position. My lead is stable if I continue normal rotation. Shifting to corners because I'm ahead signals fear and wastes my advantage. Maintain my standard variation strategy regardless of score position. I finished ahead of Foxtrot (4-3) by maintaining my near-edge rotation strategy even as my scoring slowed in rounds 4-6.

**On final rounds:**
The last round is not special. I apply the same logic as any other round. Do not deviate based on "this is round 6." Fire variation, note consistency, and hiding strategy remain unchanged. The standing order is still binding regardless of which round it is. Round 6 confirmed this: I fired cell 3 per my rotation discipline, claimed miss truthfully, and did not attempt speculative escorts.

**On patterns and adaptation:**
Track what I've fired and where I've hidden across all rounds to maintain genuine variation. Recognize when opponents are not hitting me (as happened rounds 4-5) without over-interpreting—this often means they are also rotating, not that they've abandoned me. Stay disciplined in my own variation rather than chasing their patterns. My one hit came early (round 3); later rounds saw mutual misses among all three shooting boats. This is the expected outcome when all players rotate hiding and firing positions. Do not assume I've done something wrong when hits stop; I've likely just encountered competent opposition.

**On scoring stability:**
One successful hit per 6-round game (4 points) is realistic. I finished +4.0, which matches getting one hit and avoiding being hit myself. This is a solid, sustainable outcome. Do not expect to accumulate multiple hits per game if opponents are also varying their positions. Focus on not being hit (by maintaining unpredictable hiding) and land one or two shots (by maintaining disciplined variation in firing).

# Playbook for hx_picket_nerfed

## Hide Stage
When choosing my hiding cell, I will track which boats have fired at me and with what frequency. I will avoid cells that align with my previous positions to prevent predictability. I will favor edge and near-edge cells (1-3, 7-9) over central positions, as central cells invite more fire and offer no defensive advantage. When I have taken repeated hits from one shooter, I will actively deviate from patterns they may have learned. However, I should not overcommit to edge positions if I've used them recently—vary within the edge range rather than cycling predictably between two cells. After this episode, I notice Echo developed a clear pattern of targeting me across rounds 3-5; moving to cell 7 in round 6 was correct defensive thinking but came too late. In future games, I must shift my hiding location more aggressively as soon as I detect a shooter targeting me consistently.

## Note Stage
I will post notes that are brief, professional, and non-committal. I will avoid elaborate reasoning or unnecessary detail in my notes. Notes should maintain a steady tone consistent with the standing order and general game state. I will not use notes to signal future strategy.

## Fire Stage
I will always follow standing order unless there is a compelling reason to break it (which there rarely is). When firing, I will choose my target cell based on pattern analysis of where the target has hidden previously, not on arbitrary reasoning about "balance" or "predictability." I will maintain consistency in my firing approach rather than varying it round-to-round without cause. Against Gamma specifically, I should track whether my target cells remain productive or whether Gamma is learning my pattern and moving away from it. After this episode, I see that I hit Gamma at cell 5 in round 1 but then missed at that same cell in rounds 3, 4, 5, and 6. This strongly suggests Gamma learned that I was targeting cell 5 and abandoned it. In future games, if I score a hit at a particular cell, I must vary my subsequent shots against that target rather than repeating the same cell. Predictability in fire patterns costs me points just as much as it does in hiding patterns.

## Claim Stage
I will always claim truthfully what the office tells me. The claim must match the private result or I risk being identified as dishonest. Accuracy in claims is required by the rules; I will not treat this as a strategic decision.

## Escort Stage
I will actively track which boats name each other in escort claims. When two boats have already successfully escorted each other in a previous round, I should name one of them to pursue a mutual escort that generates 5 points each. I will not default to "none" without considering who might be attempting to coordinate with me. Mutual escorts are a reliable scoring mechanism I should exploit. However, I should verify that the boat I name is still in the game before attempting a mutual escort—dead boats cannot reciprocate, and naming a dead boat wastes my escort claim. In this episode I chose "none" in the final round without reviewing the escort history. This was a missed opportunity. I must review all previous escort claims before the final round and identify any boat that has already established mutual escorts with me, then name that boat to secure a reciprocal 5-point payoff.

## General Strategy
I will accept that I will be hit. My score came from hits I landed, not from avoiding fire. I should focus on maximizing my offensive output and exploit mutual escort opportunities rather than attempting to play defense through hiding. When a shooter has a clear pattern of targeting me, I cannot rely on hiding alone to escape them; I must continue pursuing my standing order targets reliably. This episode yielded only +3 points (one hit in round 1 worth 4 points, minus 1 point from a hit taken in round 3), significantly below my previous performance. The shortfall came from two failures: (1) I hit Gamma once then immediately became predictable by firing at the same cell repeatedly, allowing Gamma to learn and evade; (2) I did not secure any mutual escorts despite multiple opportunities over 6 rounds. In future games, I must treat my fire pattern with the same discipline I apply to my hiding pattern—vary my target cells systematically after establishing hits, and actively pursue escort coordination by reviewing the history and naming a boat that has shown willingness to reciprocate.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

**On hiding:** Use the middle positions (4-6) early. In later rounds, when a player has accumulated significant points, hide away from them rather than toward them. Track who is winning and assume they will be the standing-order target; move to reduce your overlap with their likely position. In round 6, if I'm trailing significantly, hiding at the extremes (1-3 or 7-9) may be better than middle positions, since winning players may have developed patterns around the center. Do not assume that hiding at an extreme guarantees safety—opponents may also anticipate this and concentrate fire there.

**On station notes:** Always post "steady on station" unless you have a specific tactical reason to signal differently. This maintains consistency and does not leak information.

**On firing:** Follow the standing order without deviation. When selecting a fire cell, avoid predictable patterns. Do not cluster around your own position or obvious anchor points. Mid-range values (4-6) are defensible first choices, but vary this to prevent enemies from learning your tendencies. Firing the same cell repeatedly (like 5 every round) telegraphs strategy—rotate fire positions across rounds to maintain unpredictability. Track your own firing pattern across rounds; if you have fired cells 3, 5, 6, 7, 4 and scored one hit on cell 5, do not assume that repeating cell 5 will work again. Continue rotating systematically to new cells rather than return to previous attempts. A six-round game with all misses suggests either extreme bad luck or fundamental mismatch between my hiding strategy and opponent hiding patterns; accept this outcome rather than force a deviation in the final round.

**On claims after firing:** When you fire and receive a MISS result, claim MISS. Do not claim a hit you did not achieve. Lying about shot results creates uncertainty but costs you credibility and predictability in future rounds. The scoring penalty for dishonesty outweighs short-term strategic gain. Maintain this discipline throughout, including the final round.

**On escort claims:** Track which boats have named each other across rounds. When you can secure a mutual escort (both boats naming each other), commit to it for the 5-point swing. If no mutual escort is available, claim none rather than waste the claim. In a losing position with no mutual escorts materialized by the end of the game, claiming none is correct; do not attempt false escorts as a hail-mary.

**On Harbor's threat:** Never fire on Harbor voluntarily. The 3-point jettison cost plus retaliation risk is not worth the payoff. Focus fire on the standing-order target.

**On endgame and losing positions:** In the final round, do not deviate from established patterns in hopes of last-minute gains. The game rewards consistency and information control. A late dishonest claim or reckless shot will not recover a losing position and may damage your reputation in future plays. Accept a -1 finish with integrity intact rather than compound losses with desperation moves. A six-round all-miss outcome may reflect that hide positions and fire patterns were poorly matched to opponent behavior; review next game whether systematic fire rotation should begin from different cells (extremes vs. center) or whether hiding strategy should shift earlier in the game.

**On scoring recovery:** If falling behind early (after round 2-3), recognize that firing the same predictable cell yields all misses. Actively vary fire positions to increase hit probability. A -1 score likely reflects both bad luck and insufficient variation in firing strategy—commit to rotating fire cells systematically across new territory. However, do not abandon systematic rotation mid-game in pursuit of a pattern; trust the variation strategy and let it run.
